extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG) / Alice-Mayo two-step framework to determine whether claims recite patent-eligible subject matter, including how to analyze judicial exceptions and whether additional claim limitations amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is analyzed to determine whether it recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, manufacture, machine, composition) (Step 1: YES/NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: a series of acts is a 'process' (Step 1: YES); a non-transitory computer-readable medium is a 'manufacture' (Step 1: YES). Note the term 'non-transitory' excludes signals and transitory forms of transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exception identification (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A: YES/NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical algorithms, mathematical relationships/formulae, and mental steps/critical thinking (e.g., calculating/comparing) are repeatedly characterized as abstract ideas. The guidance uses examples (mathematical algorithm for scaling factor; Arrhenius equation; alarm-limit formula) to show such limitations set forth a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble limiting effect (MPEP 2111.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the preamble limits the claim: when the preamble only states a purpose or field of use it does not limit the claim; if the preamble gives 'life, meaning and vitality' it may be construed to further limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a preamble merely stating field/purpose does not add limitations (so no additional limitations beyond the abstract idea); but where the claim states the calculation is performed by 'the computer' referencing the preamble computer, the preamble 'gives life' and is limiting (see MPEP 2111.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly more analysis (Step 2B): individual elements and ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying an exception, analyze whether any additional element or combination of elements recited in the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (Step 2B: YES/NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct the Step 2B analysis for each abstract idea individually (if multiple are present) and consider both elements individually and as an ordered combination. The ordered combination can sometimes provide the required 'significantly more' where individual elements would not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere recitation of 'computer-implemented' or generic computer components performing generic functions at a high level of generality does not constitute a meaningful limitation that amounts to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states the mere recitation of 'computer-implemented' is akin to adding 'apply it' and is insufficient. Examples: reciting a computer screen and a processor for moving data, or generic computer instructions to access a database, perform calculations, and output results, when described at high-level generality, do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to a particular technological environment/field-of-use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply limiting the abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., graphical user interface) or field of use does not by itself amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Flook and other case law: restricting use of an abstract idea to a GUI or particular environment is not enough unless the claim recites meaningful additional limitations beyond mere environmental application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data gathering and post-solution activity do not add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that are merely data gathering (e.g., determining a process variable) or post-solution activity (e.g., adjusting a setting after computing a result) are not sufficient to supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: determining the value of an unspecified process variable and then adjusting an alarm limit is characterized as mere data gathering and post-solution activity that could be attached to almost any formula and therefore does not improve the technological field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of a formula does not avoid being an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical formula or relationship can be novel yet still be a judicial exception (an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the alarm-limit formula was novel but nonetheless characterized as a mathematical relationship/abstract idea (citing Mackay Radio). Novelty alone does not render a claimed mathematical formula patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination that improves technology or effects transformation can be significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: When additional limitations, taken as an ordered combination, recite a specific application that improves the functioning of a computer or another technological field or effect a transformation of an article into a different state or thing, the claim may amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: scaling and relocating text in overlapping windows improves the computer's basic display function (thus significantly more); integrating the Arrhenius equation into a computer-controlled rubber-molding press that repeatedly measures temperature and opens the press when cured both improves precision rubber molding and effects transformation of raw rubber into a cured product (Diehr example).

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level recitation of known, well-understood, routine, conventional activities weighs against eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that merely recite well-understood, routine, and conventional computer functions (e.g., accessing a database, performing calculations, initiating a timer) do not add meaningful limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is limited to computer implementation but the computer is only used for generic tasks that are routine and conventional, that computer implementation will not transform the abstract idea into eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple abstract ideas require separate Step 2B analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites multiple abstract ideas, perform the Step 2B analysis for each abstract idea individually until ineligibility for one is shown or eligibility for all is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubber-molding example explains that with multiple abstract ideas (mathematical relationship and mental steps), Step 2B must be conducted for each abstract idea in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner action guidance: how to state rejections or allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection, the examiner should identify the judicial exception by pointing to the claim elements (e.g., the formula, generating and scaling steps) and explain that those elements are abstract and why additional limitations do or do not amount to significantly more; if eligible, remarks may be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating the claim recites exceptions but is eligible due to additional limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text instruct examiners to: point to specific claim steps that are the exception (e.g., mathematical algorithm), explain similarity to court-found abstract ideas, note whether preamble limits the claim, and explain why additional limitations fail to add significantly more (e.g., mere data gathering, field-of-use, generic computer functions) or why they do (ordered combination that improves technology).
